title: Gryzzlbox

jokes.text: Leslie's defeatist opening monologue — 'It's impossible. It's not gonna work in a million years. It's pointless. I give up.' — followed by Ben's deadpan 'Good attitude, honey.'
jokes.setup: Leslie spirals into an increasingly dramatic list of reasons why her mission is hopeless.
jokes.punchline: Ben's flat, affectionate 'Good attitude, honey' punctures her spiral with perfect comic timing.
jokes.explanation: Works because both halves are perfectly in character — Leslie's over-the-top catastrophizing and Ben's loving but bone-dry response. The rhythm is tight. Slightly familiar territory for the show but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is it. This is the end. We've lost everything. The parks department is finished. I've failed as a director, I've failed as a leader, and I've failed as a human being. We might as well just shut down the whole city and move to a deserted island because civilization is over.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Or we could just try again tomorrow.

jokes.text: Leslie summarizes her entire pitch to the landowners as: 'Please, give us the land. It would be so nice.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is framing her argument as legitimate civic persuasion against a billion-dollar corporation.
jokes.punchline: Her actual argument boils down to a polite plea with zero leverage — hilariously self-aware.
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical — the comedy is entirely in the deflation from 'basic argument' to that guileless plea. Strong character integration since only Leslie would state this with such earnest transparency.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, here's what we're going to do. We're going to make a website. And on that website, we're going to list all the reasons why this corporation is bad. Then we're going to email it to everyone we know. And if that doesn't work, we'll make a second website.

jokes.text: A delivery drone arrives at Leslie and Ben's door, causing both to shriek and Ben to declare 'The robots have come for us.'
jokes.setup: They've just been discussing how they can't compete with Gryzzl's billions.
jokes.punchline: The comedic timing of the drone's arrival immediately after their conversation, plus their panicked overreaction.
jokes.explanation: Great structural payoff — the very thing they were discussing manifests on their doorstep. The visual of the drone plus their screaming sells the absurdity. Rewatch value because the transition from the conversation to the knock is so tight.

dialogue.speaker: Robotic Voice
dialogue.line: Open the door.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Did that... did that just talk to us?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know. Should we open it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No! Why would we open a door that's telling us to open it?

jokes.text: Ben says 'I made fun of you when you said it would happen, but your novel has come true,' implying Leslie wrote a dystopian novel about robot deliveries.
jokes.setup: Chaos of drone arriving at door.
jokes.punchline: The casual reveal that Leslie wrote a predictive dystopian novel, treated as totally normal background information.
jokes.explanation: Excellent background gag — implies a whole unseen dimension of Leslie's obsessive civic anxiety that she turned into fiction. Completely earned character comedy. The casualness of the delivery is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Is this it? Is this how it starts? The robot apocalypse? I knew it!

jokes.text: Leslie's deadpan talking head: 'Okay, so they also have a squadron of flying robots giving presents to everyone. We're screwed.'
jokes.setup: The drone delivered a gift; the situation has escalated dramatically.
jokes.punchline: 'We're screwed.' — delivered as a matter-of-fact business assessment.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the contrast between the elaborate corporate display and Leslie's flat two-word verdict is the whole joke. Works as punctuation for the cold open.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I may have made fun of Ben's novel about robots taking over the world. But in my defense, at the time, it seemed ridiculous.

jokes.text: Tom explains he's creating new dishes to distract himself from imagining 'the marathon bone sesh' Lucy and Conrad are probably having.
jokes.setup: Tom claims he's doing new dishes just to stay busy while Lucy visits her boyfriend.
jokes.punchline: 'the marathon bone sesh they're probably having' — shockingly frank euphemism delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Very Tom — the combination of vulnerability and crass specificity. 'Marathon bone sesh' is a weirdly specific and quotable phrase that perfectly captures his anxious-bro energy. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I guess that's it then. Gryzzl wins. They have drones. We don't have drones. Drones are the future. I accept this outcome.

jokes.text: Tom reads Andy's contract: 'Wait, this says they only pay you a hundred bucks a week?' Andy: 'Yeah, but all I really do is goof around all day. Write, produce, and direct a TV show. Plus, I act in it, and I do sets, props, wardrobe. At the end, I drive everybody home... a hundred bucks a week—that's pretty fair.'
jokes.setup: Tom discovers Andy makes only $100/week and expresses shock
jokes.punchline: Andy lists an enormous amount of labor he does, then circles back to validating the terrible pay
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The escalating list of Andy's actual job responsibilities — write, produce, direct, act, sets, props, wardrobe, DRIVE EVERYONE HOME — followed by his earnest conclusion that $100/week is 'pretty fair' is a perfect character joke. Only Andy Dwyer, whose self-worth is essentially zero, could deliver this. The escalation builds perfectly, the driving-everyone-home detail is a superb button, and it's highly quotable. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is a seared foie gras terrine with a blackberry gastrique, micro greens, and a quenelle of burrata cheese, all served on a bed of—

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Done.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: —edible flowers.

jokes.text: Tom describes his plan to be Andy's agent: 'I'll put all my energy into renegotiating your contract. I won't even think about Lucy and Conrad and his stupid crunches that he probably does.'
jokes.setup: Tom announces he'll distract himself from jealousy by becoming Andy's agent.
jokes.punchline: He immediately undermines this by thinking specifically about Conrad's crunches.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because the denial IS the obsession. 'His stupid crunches that he probably does' escalates the specificity in a funny direction — Conrad has become a physical ideal in Tom's mind.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm trying new dishes because I want to impress people. You know, show off my culinary skills.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Plus, between you and me, I get jealous when other guys cook for their girlfriends. Like, that should be my thing, you know? I should be the one making her food, making her happy...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I just don't want some other dude up in there with his spatula, okay?

jokes.text: Immediately after Tom says he won't think about Conrad's crunches, cut to Tom doing crunches and saying 'I should probably do some crunches.'
jokes.setup: Tom just declared he wouldn't think about Conrad's exercise routine.
jokes.punchline: He's literally doing crunches.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect structural economy — the callback lands within seconds of the setup and requires zero additional words. The audience anticipates the joke from the moment Tom mentions Conrad's crunches; the immediate visual confirmation is the payoff. One of the tightest structural jokes in the episode. Justifies an 8+ score: it's comparable in structure/economy quality to the anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I just goof around all day. I don't actually do anything.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You coordinate between multiple city departments, you've streamlined our permitting process, you've managed multi-million dollar budgets, and you've successfully lobbied the city council for three major initiatives.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but like, goofing around though.

jokes.text: Andy's response to Tom doing crunches on him: 'Ow! Andy, my tum tum!'
jokes.setup: Tom randomly starts doing crunches, apparently on Andy or near him.
jokes.punchline: Tom's self-referential complaint ('my tum tum') reveals he's doing crunches ON Andy or bumped into him.
jokes.explanation: Decent physical button on the crunch joke. 'My tum tum' is an endearingly absurd phrase for Tom to use, but the joke is fairly low-stakes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm the host, I'm the producer, I'm the director, I'm the camera operator, I'm the boom mic guy, I'm the lighting designer, I'm the editor, I'm the guy who gets the coffee... $100 a week seems fair.

jokes.text: Donna reveals her GryzzlBox contained two honey bears and sugar plums — which are private pet names she and Joe call each other that they only use in texts and calls.
jokes.setup: Donna says Gryzzl has crossed a line with its data-mining gifts.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Gryzzl somehow mined their private pet names — 'Honeybear' and 'Sugar Plum' — from private communications.
jokes.explanation: This joke does triple duty: it's funny (the names are adorable and absurd), it makes the privacy invasion feel personal and real rather than abstract, AND it's a genuine character moment for Donna showing vulnerability. The addendum 'Aww' from a bystander followed by her immediate defensiveness ('Yeah, we're adorable, but this is creepy') is perfectly structured. Earns the 8+ because it's funny AND thematically resonant — the humor is completely earned by character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm not going to think about Lucy's boyfriend. I'm just going to move on with my life.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But I wonder what Conrad's doing right now. Is he thinking about Lucy? Does he call her 'Luce' or 'Lucy'? I bet he calls her 'Luce.' That's so intimate. Do they have a song? They probably have a song.

jokes.text: Leslie's GryzzlBox contains: Joe Biden's book 'Biden the Rails: 1001 Poems Inspired by My Travels Through Amtrak's Northeast Corridor'
jokes.setup: Leslie opens her box to reveal hyper-personalized gifts.
jokes.punchline: A fake Joe Biden book that is absurdly specific — poetry about Amtrak — and yet completely plausible as something Leslie would treasure.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The fake book title is a perfect intersection of three running jokes: Leslie's obsession with Biden, Biden's real-life Amtrak obsession (genuine character detail), and the absurdist specificity of 1,001 poems about train travel. The extra beat of someone asking 'A thousand?' nails it further. This is exactly the kind of joke that rewards show knowledge while also being accessible. Highly quotable title. Genuine originality — this specific combination could only exist in Parks and Rec.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm gonna start working out. I'm gonna get huge muscles, just like Conrad.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ow! Ow! Ow! My back! My back! Somebody call a doctor! Wahhh!

jokes.text: Leslie's box also contains 'A poster of the Supreme Court Justices sipping the Friends milkshake'
jokes.setup: GryzzlBox items are revealed one by one as hyper-personalized.
jokes.punchline: An increasingly specific piece of fan merchandise combining two of Leslie's loves — government and pop culture nostalgia.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from the Biden book to THIS — a poster of Supreme Court Justices drinking the iconic Friends milkshake — is a brilliant collision of Leslie's two personality pillars (government obsession, 90s pop culture love). The specificity of 'the Friends milkshake' (the Central Perk giant cup) makes it funnier than a generic crossover. Strong originality and exceptional character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: We call each other 'Snuggle Bug' and 'Cuddle Monster.' It's very cute.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: That's adorable.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Yeah, it is. And then he beats me.

jokes.text: Donna: 'Gryzzl is going down. You wanna put me on blast? I'ma put you on Front Street.' Leslie: 'I don't understand what that means, but I think I get the context, and I love it.'
jokes.setup: Donna delivers a fierce declaration of war against Gryzzl in her own slang.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's enthusiastic partial comprehension — she gets the vibe but not the words, and endorses it wholesale.
jokes.explanation: Both halves are essential. Donna's battle cry is great on its own, but Leslie's response ('I don't understand what that means but I think I get the context and I love it') is where the real comedy lives — it's a perfectly Leslie thing to say, it's generous, warm, and funny all at once. Highly quotable. The structure is a two-beat joke where both beats land. Earns 8+ because of genuine character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, they sent me 'Joe Biden: A Life of Valor and Tremendous Accomplishments.' This is perfect!

jokes.text: April is asked to give a welcome speech to new interns. She initially says 'No, go away.'
jokes.setup: Ben politely asks April to welcome interns.
jokes.punchline: April's flat, monosyllabic refusal.
jokes.explanation: Classic April, economical and perfectly in character. Slightly predictable — April refusing to do something nice is well-trodden territory — but the bluntness still works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm starting a new initiative called 'Parks and Rec-reation,' where we combine municipal government with top 40 hits. Every pothole we fill gets a Beyoncé song.

jokes.text: April's talking head: 'I started here when I was 20, and now I'm old and gross and directionless. Those kids are me ten years ago, and this internship is the videotape from The Ring. It's too late for me. I've seen too much. But maybe I can save them.'
jokes.setup: April reflects on what she should tell the new interns.
jokes.punchline: Her entire framing of the internship as a horror-movie curse she must warn others about — with the unearned hero's journey twist of 'maybe I can save them.'
jokes.explanation: This is the strongest purely comedic monologue in the episode. The Ring comparison is unexpected and perfectly calibrated to April's sensibility — it frames civic service as existential dread. 'It's too late for me. I've seen too much.' is quotable and funny in isolation. The sudden pivot to 'But maybe I can save them' — treating herself as a reluctant hero — is a masterful tonal shift that subverts the nihilism. This earns a high score: original, character-perfect, economical, and the structure escalates and then turns beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You want to take this outside?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Outside? Why would we go outside? It's cold, and there's bugs. Plus, I have a really great idea for a fall festival that I want to tell you about right now.

jokes.text: April's 'welcome speech' to interns: 'You're all gonna die in here!'
jokes.setup: April's internal monologue about saving the interns sets up a misleading expectation that she'll be helpful.
jokes.punchline: Her actual speech is just a warning cry that they're all doomed.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the talking head. The humor works on pure structural economy — the entire buildup of 'maybe I can save them' resolves into her most malevolent possible action. The mock-heroism of the confessional makes the nihilistic punchline even funnier. Five words, perfect delivery implied. Highly quotable on its own. Earns high score as the culmination of a well-built two-part joke.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My therapist says I should list positive things about myself. So here goes: I'm punctual, I have nice handwriting, I've never been to jail, I don't have any diseases that I know of, I'm a good listener, I'm a loyal friend, I have a good sense of humor, and I smell nice.

jokes.text: At the town meeting, a resident reveals Gryzzl sent her husband 'three boxes of genital cream to his office.'
jokes.setup: Leslie opens a public forum about Gryzzl's privacy invasions.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'three boxes of genital cream' and the double embarrassment of it going to his office.
jokes.explanation: Good community-meeting cringe comedy. The 'three boxes' detail is funny (why three?), and the office delivery amplifies the embarrassment. Establishes the running gag of increasingly personal GryzzlBox reveals.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to say something positive about myself. I'm April Ludgate, and I'm a talented, intelligent, and valuable member of society.

dialogue.speaker: Therapist
dialogue.line: That's wonderful, April. How does that make you feel?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Like I'm lying to myself. But in a healthy way.

jokes.text: Same resident: 'My husband's splotchy genitals are no one's business, except for his, mine, and his many genital doctors.'
jokes.setup: She complained about the genital cream delivery.
jokes.punchline: 'His many genital doctors' — a horrifying escalation that implies a whole medical history nobody asked for.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'genital cream' to 'his many genital doctors' (plural, implying a team of specialists) is a masterclass in using specificity to generate horror-comedy. 'Splotchy' is a committed and disgusting word choice. The overshare structure — she tries to defend his privacy by revealing far more — is a great irony. Highly quotable as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about my time as an intern. It was like being cursed by a horror movie artifact. Every day I thought it would kill me, but it just made me stronger and more bitter.

jokes.text: Another resident reveals his private hobby: 'toy pigs dressed like movie stars.' He names one: 'Ham-uel L. Jackson from the movie Pork Fiction, it's extremely rare, and I am keeping it.'
jokes.setup: A resident complains that his private hobby was exposed by Gryzzl.
jokes.punchline: The pig pun names — 'Ham-uel L. Jackson,' 'Pork Fiction' — and his insistence on keeping the extremely rare gift despite his outrage.
jokes.explanation: The pig pun names are genuinely inspired — 'Ham-uel L. Jackson' and 'Pork Fiction' are very funny portmanteaus. But the structural joke on top of the pun — he's simultaneously condemning Gryzzl and refusing to give back the gift — is what elevates this. The comedy of his hypocrisy undermines his own outrage beautifully. 'Extremely rare' makes it even funnier. One of the most quotable moments in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've decided to take the interns under my wing. I'm going to be a mentor figure, guide them, help them grow.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: BOO! Get out of here! This is my office now!

jokes.text: A teenager complains that her box contained Virginia Woolf novels, and now her friends Miley and Haley know she reads. 'What if they tell Evan?'
jokes.setup: Residents describe personal items Gryzzl mined from their data.
jokes.punchline: Her privacy concern is specifically about Evan finding out she's literate — a perfect teenage social priority parody.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical observation about teenage social performance — the humor comes from the inversion of expected privacy concerns (not embarrassed by data-mining, embarrassed by being smart). 'What if they tell Evan?' is the perfect specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I can't believe you people are invading my privacy like this. It's outrageous!

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: My husband has been suffering from a severe case of hemorrhoids for three weeks now. The bleeding is just uncontrollable, and the itching is so intense he can barely sit down. His doctor says it might require surgery.

jokes.text: Leslie talking head: 'The next domino to fall? Ron Swanson.' Cut to: 'Actually, this is Tom Sell-oink, but, you know, close enough.'
jokes.setup: Leslie builds dramatic anticipation about getting Ron Swanson on her side.
jokes.punchline: Cut to the pig figure — Tom Sell-oink — which the resident clarifies is not Ron Swanson.
jokes.explanation: Great structural joke — mockumentary editing creates a fake callback where the 'next person we see' is the pig figure being held up, not Ron. The name 'Tom Sell-oink' (Tom Selleck + oink) is a bonus pun. Uses the pig collection callback effectively. The beat 'close enough' earns a laugh through Leslie's wishful thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I collect pigs that look like famous movie stars. My prize pig looks just like Samuel L. Jackson.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I call him Samuel L. Pigson.

jokes.text: The resident immediately takes the pig back from Leslie: 'Actually, I'm gonna need that back.'
jokes.setup: Leslie used the pig figure as a prop in her monologue.
jokes.punchline: He reclaims his 'extremely rare' collectible with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: Effective button on the pig running gag. Short, economical, earns a laugh from commitment to the bit. Slightly predictable but executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I can't believe you people are invading my privacy like this. This is a violation of my constitutional rights.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: But I have to say, this gift basket is amazing. These are my favorite cookies.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: photo album hits include 'First Trip to the Dentist,' 'Sonia Tries Pizza,' and 'Waterpark Vomit Chain Reaction.'
jokes.setup: Ron is sharing a February 2016 photo album — framed as mundane domestic life.
jokes.punchline: 'Waterpark Vomit Chain Reaction' — delivered in the same cheerful tone as the wholesome milestones.
jokes.explanation: The joke's genius is in the escalation structure: two sweet, wholesome milestone titles followed by 'Waterpark Vomit Chain Reaction,' delivered with equal parental pride. Ron treating a public vomit disaster as a cherished memory worth photographing is perfect for his character — stoic, unsentimental, but deeply invested in his family. Highly quotable. Earns 8+ through originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Young citizen
dialogue.line: I'm really concerned about my privacy online. I don't want people knowing my personal information.

dialogue.speaker: Young citizen
dialogue.line: Like, I'd be mortified if my friends found out I read literature.

jokes.text: Leslie's partner asks why Ron would photograph 'Waterpark Vomit Chain Reaction.' Ron's response: 'Why would you not?'
jokes.setup: The vomit chain reaction photo is questioned.
jokes.punchline: Ron's baffled counter-question — his logic is unassailable from his perspective.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words ('Why would you not?') extend the joke at no cost. Ron's cheerful bewilderment that this wouldn't be photographed is completely consistent with his character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, it's not that hard. You just need to show the pig some affection and—

dialogue.speaker: Pig collector
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! That's my pig!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just demonstrating—

dialogue.speaker: Pig collector
dialogue.line: Nobody touches Mr. Truffles but me!

jokes.text: Ron shows a picture of his son 'at a recent moment in his life' — it's a completely redacted/blacked-out image.
jokes.setup: As requested, Ron provides a picture of his son.
jokes.punchline: The image is entirely blacked out — he's protecting his child's privacy to a paranoid degree.
jokes.explanation: Excellent visual gag that only works because of Ron's character. His refusal to let anyone see a photograph of his son — even a photograph! — is a perfect extension of his paranoid libertarianism. The line 'What, I'm just gonna carry around pictures of my child where anyone could see them?' establishes his logic and makes it funnier. Visually satisfying and character-perfect. Earns 8+ for character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Here's me at age five with my first dog. Here's me at seven with a scraped knee. Here's me at nine covered in mud. Here's me at eleven with a rash that the dermatologist said was 'concerning.' Here's me at thirteen with what I'm pretty sure was a minor infection. Here's me at fifteen covered in what I can only describe as a biological hazard.

jokes.text: Ron responds to Gryzzl's data-mining with: 'I have no reaction to this.' Then explains he doesn't judge private businesses and that people foolish enough to carry tracking devices deserve what they get.
jokes.setup: Leslie expects Ron to be outraged by Gryzzl's privacy invasion.
jokes.punchline: Ron's libertarian principles lead him to defend the very thing everyone expected him to oppose.
jokes.explanation: A good Ron joke in that his principles are internally consistent even when they're frustrating. The expectation that he'd be Leslie's most natural ally is subverted by his own ideology. Slightly predictable for longtime viewers but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would you show me a photo of your child? That's a security risk. Now I know what they look like. If they ever go missing, I could identify them immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You've essentially given me a dossier. I could find them anywhere.

jokes.text: Ron says he's spent time with Gryzzl's lawyers and they 'keep it 100,' delivered in Ron's extremely formal diction.
jokes.setup: Ron defends Gryzzl's legal team.
jokes.punchline: Ron Swanson using the slang 'keep it 100' in his stiff, formal register.
jokes.explanation: The character contrast — Ron Swanson saying 'keep it 100' — is the entire joke, and it's a very good one. His apparent absorption of Gryzzl's millennial vocabulary while maintaining his stoic demeanor is absurdly funny. Economy of execution is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Those Gryzzl lawyers are relentless. They've got me in a corner.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I guess you could say... they're really 'slaying' me right now. No cap, fam. That's what the kids say, right?

jokes.text: Ron and Donna go undercover. Ron introduces himself as 'Gregory Strong,' assistant-turned-lover, with a romance that 'sent shockwaves through my architecture firm. But it feels so right.' — delivered in Ron's wooden, militaristic manner.
jokes.setup: Ron and Donna need cover identities to tour Gryzzl.
jokes.punchline: Ron's attempt at performing a romantic backstory in his completely flat, unconvincing way.
jokes.explanation: Ron performing romantic tenderness is inherently funny because of the character mismatch. 'Sent shockwaves through my architecture firm' delivered in his stoic voice is perfect. Donna's coaching 'Steady' suggests Ron is barely holding it together, adding a visual comedy layer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so my name is Brenda Withers, I'm a dental hygienist from Muncie, Indiana. I have two cats named Mr. Whiskers and Princess Fluffington. I'm divorced, but it was amicable. My ex-husband Brad and I still text on birthdays. He's remarried now to a woman named Tiffany, and honestly, I'm happy for them. They have a golden retriever named Biscuit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, why would any of that matter for going undercover?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because details make it real, Ben. People trust specificity.

jokes.text: April asks a new intern named Mike what brought him to Parks. He says he loves parks more than anything and has been a summer camp counselor since age 13. April's response: 'Ugh. Gross.'
jokes.setup: April is running a brutal orientation meeting, apparently looking for cynicism.
jokes.punchline: Mike's enthusiastic, wholesome answer physically disgusts April.
jokes.explanation: Classic April. The joke is simple and slightly worn but executed with perfect economy. Her revulsion at genuine enthusiasm is a reliable character note.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I hate it. Parks are just where people go to die.

jokes.text: Intern: 'The only thing I love more than parks is recreation.' April's reaction. Intern: 'No, I just needed college credit.'
jokes.setup: After two earnest interns, a third says she loves parks AND recreation — the perfect answer for this job
jokes.punchline: Immediate backtrack: she was joking, she just needs credit; even better, she's not even in college
jokes.explanation: Expertly constructed misdirection with a second layer. The 'nothing, I just needed college credit' reversal from the perfect-sounding answer is already good; then it doubles down: she's not in college. This escalation gives the joke a satisfying extra beat. Also meta-self-referential given the show's title.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Parks and Recreation is the most important field of study. It shapes communities, creates opportunities for public engagement, and fundamentally transforms how we experience our shared spaces.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's literally the only reason I'm here.

jokes.text: An intern says the only reason she's there is for college credit. April asks what she's studying. 'Nothing. College is stupid.' April asks who made her do this. 'My parents.' April: 'What are they like?' 'Well, my mom's the devil and my dad's a dumb doctor.' April immediately: 'I feel like you have almost zero potential. I think that's cool.'
jokes.setup: April has been appalled by sincere interns and is looking for someone like herself.
jokes.punchline: April identifies the nihilistic intern as a kindred spirit and takes her under her wing.
jokes.explanation: This entire exchange is well-built. 'My mom's the devil and my dad's a dumb doctor' is funny but the punchline is April recognizing zero potential as a virtue — a perfect inversion of mentorship. April has found her mirror image and is inexplicably proud of it. The 'I feel like you have almost zero potential. I think that's cool' line is genuinely quotable and captures April's dark inversion of normal values. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What are your parents like?

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Oh, my mom's a devil and my dad's an idiot.

jokes.text: The intern (Jen) says 'my mom's the devil and my dad's a dumb doctor.' Other intern: 'Oh, my dad's a doctor.' Jen: 'Shut up.'
jokes.setup: April is quizzing Jen about her background; Jen describes her parents dismissively
jokes.punchline: A well-meaning intern tries to connect over the doctor dad detail; Jen shuts him down with two words
jokes.explanation: The economy of 'Shut up' as the entire response is perfect. Mike's guileless attempt to bond and Jen's immediate dismissal is a quick, effective character beat. 'My mom's the devil' is also a great throwaway.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Jen has no skills, no experience, and no discernible future. It's actually kind of appealing.

jokes.text: April to Jen: 'I feel like you have almost zero potential. I think that's cool.'
jokes.setup: April has been probing Jen for anti-establishment qualities
jokes.punchline: April compliments Jen specifically for having 'almost zero potential' — inverting the entire purpose of the internship interview
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great April Ludgate line. The compliment is 'almost zero potential' — not 'no potential' but 'almost zero,' which is even more precisely specific. April sees a kindred spirit in someone who has no investment in the system. The inversion of conventional mentorship values is sharp and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Being an agent is so easy. You just take a percentage of everything your clients make, and you don't have to do any work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait... that's my business model.

jokes.text: Johnny Karate show scene: 'Puppy-Hating Dan' steals Johnny's guitar. 'And you put farts in my lunch.' The villain ultimately confesses to everything.
jokes.setup: The Johnny Karate show is performing an episode in production.
jokes.punchline: 'And you put farts in my lunch' — as an equal grievance to guitar theft, delivered in the show's mock-heroic register.
jokes.explanation: The Johnny Karate show is inherently funny as a concept — it perfectly captures Andy's absurdist worldview in TV form. 'Farts in my lunch' has the childlike specificity of real kids' TV grievances. The villain's immediate total capitulation ('I'll admit to everything. You win again, Macklin.') is also funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so you know that famous line from Casablanca? 'Here's looking at you, kid.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, that's the one where Rick says it to Ilsa at the end, right? Actually, did you know that Humphrey Bogart was only 25 years older than Ingrid Bergman? And the studio was worried about their age difference!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: ...I was just trying to quote the movie.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Also, Bogart's character was originally supposed to die in the scene, but they changed it because test audiences wanted a happier ending!

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'I love being Andy's agent. He does all the work, and I get 10% just for showing up. It's like a chef at a restaurant, making all the food, and then the owner gets a profit — which is my other job!'
jokes.setup: Tom celebrates his new role as Andy's agent.
jokes.punchline: His analogy accidentally perfectly describes exploitation — and he's completely oblivious, then cheerfully reveals he IS a restaurant owner.
jokes.explanation: The accidental self-indictment of the analogy is the whole joke — Tom is unwittingly explaining labor exploitation, then immediately reveals he's the restaurant owner he just described. 'Man, I really got things figured out' as a button on this self-incrimination is perfect. Strong character integration — Tom's entrepreneurial ego blinds him to the irony.

dialogue.speaker: Station Manager
dialogue.line: I discovered a celebrity! It's Ben Wyatt!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, really? THE Ben Wyatt?

dialogue.speaker: Station Manager
dialogue.line: Well, no. It's a different Ben Wyatt. He works at a shoe store.

jokes.text: Station manager name-drops people he's 'made': 'Pep Wiley, Chuck Warschank, Selena Gomez — I made them.' Tom: 'You discovered Selena Gomez?' Manager: 'Different Selena Gomez.'
jokes.setup: The station manager boasts about his history of launching careers.
jokes.punchline: 'Different Selena Gomez' — he's not claiming the pop star, just someone with the same name, completely deflating his brag.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misdirection joke. The name-drop creates a specific expectation; 'Different Selena Gomez' destroys it completely in three words. This is a classic comedy structure executed with perfect economy. Highly quotable, works completely out of context. Earns 8+ clearly — it's in the class of the 8.0 anchor example.

jokes.text: April asks Jen what she wanted to be when she was little. 'A scary mermaid that lures sailors to their death.' April: 'Okay, side note, I'm gonna file papers to adopt you as my child, so keep an eye out for that.'
jokes.setup: April is trying to determine what Jen should do with her life instead of the internship.
jokes.punchline: The siren fantasy is so perfectly April-coded that she decides to legally adopt this teenager.
jokes.explanation: Multiple reasons this excels: 'Scary mermaid that lures sailors to their death' is an inspired, specific, and very funny childhood dream. April's response — immediate adoption papers — is a perfect non sequitur that lands as completely logical given her character. The casual 'keep an eye out for that' treats a bizarre legal action as an afterthought. Both lines are quotable. This interaction encapsulates why April is one of TV's great comic characters.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm adopting you. I've already filled out the paperwork.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, but I'm going to.

jokes.text: April: 'Okay, side note, I'm gonna file papers to adopt you as my child, so keep an eye out for that.'
jokes.setup: April has just heard Jen describe wanting to be a death-luring mermaid
jokes.punchline: April's response to this dark childhood dream is to immediately begin adoption proceedings
jokes.explanation: The adoption announcement as a direct response to 'a scary mermaid that lures sailors to their death' perfectly captures April's value system. 'So keep an eye out for that' as a breezy afterthought about legal adoption proceedings is a great button. The joke rewards Jen for her dark answer and reveals April's deep identification with it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If you don't want to do the internship, you could always become a professional snake charmer or learn to forge medieval weapons.

jokes.text: April tells Jen instead of the internship, she should do something fun 'like trying to control birds with your mind or posting internet comments as Michael Jackson's ghost.'
jokes.setup: April is advising Jen to pursue more meaningful activities than a Parks internship.
jokes.punchline: Her examples of 'fun' alternatives are completely deranged non-options.
jokes.explanation: Both examples are specifically April-calibrated absurdism — one quasi-mystical (bird mind control), one internet-era ghoulish (MJ ghost commenting). The specificity of 'posting internet comments as Michael Jackson's ghost' is inspired. High originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl employee
dialogue.line: We track everything. Your location, your purchases, your search history, your conversations.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're just... casually mentioning this?

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl employee
dialogue.line: Of course. It's in the terms and conditions.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Nobody reads those!

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl employee
dialogue.line: We know.

jokes.text: Roscoe shows Ron and Donna the GryzzlVibe mood app: 'The cameras on your phones are always on, whether you're using them or not.' Ron and Donna's visible alarm.
jokes.setup: Roscoe gives an enthusiastic demo of Gryzzl's new mood-tracking technology.
jokes.punchline: Casual revelation that cameras are always on — said cheerfully — while the audience (and Ron/Donna) process the horror.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the contrast between Roscoe's breezy delivery and the genuinely alarming content. Effective cringe-comedy moment where the punchline is a real surveillance horror wrapped in startup cheerfulness.

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: We collect data on everything - shopping habits, browsing history, pharmaceutical purchases...

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: You know, tampons, pads, that sort of thing.

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: It's just... data.

jokes.text: Roscoe explains the elaborate mood-sensing app's ultimate purpose: it directs sad people to coffee and happy people also to coffee. 'So it's really just a coffee sales app.' — Ron. 'Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, we're developing with Starbucks.'
jokes.setup: Roscoe presents GryzzlVibe as a revolutionary mood-sensing technology.
jokes.punchline: The entire elaborate system resolves to: sell people coffee. Ron's understated deflation is the delivery mechanism.
jokes.explanation: Great satirical joke about tech industry grandiosity hiding trivial commercial goals. The deflation is perfectly structured — the longer Roscoe talks, the bigger the expected revelation, making 'coffee' even funnier. Ron's flat restatement as a question ('So it's really just a coffee sales app') is the delivery mechanism. Good tech industry satire.

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: Gryzzl isn't scary. They're just a company that wants to help people.

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: Sure, they monitor every purchase you make, track your location 24/7, predict your behavior before you know what you're going to do, and have access to all your personal data. But that's not scary, that's just business.

jokes.text: Roscoe: 'Oh, hells yeah, dog-man. Our super rad algorithm searches all your texts, calls, banking, medical records, blah, blah, blah...'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Roscoe directly if they're data-mining
jokes.punchline: Roscoe confirms comprehensive surveillance of medical records and banking with 'hells yeah, dog-man' and a dismissive 'blah blah blah' as though it's mundane
jokes.explanation: The horror of the surveillance confession is amplified by Roscoe's casual enthusiasm. 'Blah, blah, blah' treating 'banking, medical records' as boring list items is the key comedic choice — he doesn't realize these are alarming. The 'hells yeah, dog-man' opening is the tone-setting punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We should do a debate on television.

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: Television? That's adorable. You still think people watch television.

jokes.text: Roscoe tells Donna: 'we might know you better than you know yourself, Leslie.' Donna: 'How did you know it was me?' Roscoe: 'Oh, there's about 40 different ways.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Donna are undercover. Roscoe has just been casually listing surveillance capabilities.
jokes.punchline: Roscoe sees through Donna's cover instantly (calling her Leslie) and when she asks how, the answer is '40 different ways' — implying the level of surveillance makes a disguise irrelevant.
jokes.explanation: The joke lands on multiple levels: the futility of their undercover operation, the terrifying depth of surveillance, and Roscoe's cheerful obliviousness to how unsettling this is. '40 different ways' delivered casually is genuinely funny and also a bit horrifying — the right tone for this satirical subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: I'm Perd Hapley, and I have some news. On today's show, we'll be talking to the guests we've booked to be on the show.

jokes.text: Roscoe describes Gryzzl's mission: 'we just wanna learn everything about everyone and track them wherever they go and anticipate what they're about to do.' Says it as if describing something wholesome.
jokes.setup: Roscoe is trying to reassure Leslie/Donna that there's 'nothing scary about Gryzzl.'
jokes.punchline: His reassurance is the most unsettling possible summary of a surveillance company's goals, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the tone-content mismatch — a total surveillance agenda presented as neighborly and chill. 'Nothing scary about Gryzzl' + an actually scary description. The structure is tight and the satirical point is clear.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You missed the contract change on page forty-seven.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was up until 3 AM watching the original trilogy again.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I heard you sleep-talking last night. You kept saying 'Help me, Obi-Wan Kenobi. You're my only hope.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's actually beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It was disturbing.

jokes.text: Judge Perd Hapley introduces his show: 'Tonight, on The Perdples Court, we will have the guests that have been booked for tonight's show...' and continues restating information with meta-circularity.
jokes.setup: Perd opens his legal debate show.
jokes.punchline: Perd's defining characteristic — he can only state what is self-evidently happening — reaches maximum density in his hosting duties. 'Who will win? I don't know yet. Which is what makes this a court show.'
jokes.explanation: Perd Hapley's empty tautological announcements are one of the show's great recurring joke structures. 'Who will win? I don't know yet. Which is what makes this a court show.' is the clearest expression of his character in the episode. Perfect character integration — no other character could say this.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't understand the appeal. A bunch of wizards waving sticks around in space?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's not a story, that's a weapon malfunction.

jokes.text: Ben tells Leslie not to humiliate herself on TV. Leslie's response: 'public humiliation on live television' is the tool she plans to use — against Gryzzl, not herself.
jokes.setup: Leslie says she needs one more thing Americans respect — set up to sound like she's about to say something principled.
jokes.punchline: 'Public humiliation on live television' — reveals her strategy is essentially a PR attack, and Ben's worried she's about to embarrass herself.
jokes.explanation: Light misdirection — sets up a noble speech and delivers a tactical confession instead. Works as a character beat showing Leslie's pragmatic ruthlessness beneath the idealism.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Andy, I need you to create a new character for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, how about... Master Dragon?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's too specific. Something more generic.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Alright... Sensei Strike?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Still too creative.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, uh... Karate Guy?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You're getting there.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How about just... Punch?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Perfect.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'The one thing Americans respect more than anything else: public humiliation on live television.' Ben: 'Leslie, don't humiliate yourself on television.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is building to a triumphant strategic declaration
jokes.punchline: Her 'secret weapon' is public humiliation, and Ben's response is to assume she means self-humiliation — suggesting this has happened before
jokes.explanation: The joke hinges on Ben's immediate assumption that 'public humiliation' = Leslie will humiliate herself. His warning implies deep experiential knowledge of Leslie Knope on television. Good character comedy with an implicit backstory.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I've accomplished many things in my life. I've built a canoe from scratch. I've fished for sturgeon. I've negotiated with drug lords.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: And I once sat in a car for three days straight without moving or speaking to anyone.

jokes.text: Ron reveals the privacy clause was hidden in Amendment C, Addendum 14, which redirects to an appendix, which redirects to another appendix, which contains a sub-footnote — all buried in a 500-page document.
jokes.setup: Ron arrives with evidence that the data-mining IS technically legal.
jokes.punchline: The absurd depth of the document maze required to hide one sentence — and the implication that Gryzzl knew exactly what they were doing.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of Ron dramatically flipping through pages to reveal this deliberately obscured clause is good. The bureaucratic maze of appendices and sub-footnotes is a funny way to dramatize a real phenomenon (terms of service obfuscation).

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't believe in contracts. They're a sign of distrust between people.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If I ever had to sign a contract, I'd use a fake name. Something like... Turnip Slamdunk.

jokes.text: Ron reveals the amendment was dated December 18, 2015 — the opening day of Star Wars: Episode VII. 'You were muttering that date in your sleep for months. They knew you'd be distracted. That's how they slipped it in.'
jokes.setup: The revision date seems suspicious — Ron has figured out why Leslie missed it.
jokes.punchline: Gryzzl timed the amendment to the most culturally distracting event in Leslie's world — a corporate gambit that required knowing Star Wars fans' behavior patterns.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. It works simultaneously as: (1) a great character joke about Ben's obsessive Star Wars fandom (muttering the date in his sleep), (2) a genuinely clever satirical point about corporations exploiting public distraction, and (3) an absurdist extension of the tech dystopia theme. The logic is internally coherent while being completely hilarious. 'She was muttering that date in her sleep for months' — wait, who does that? Ben does. That's perfect characterization. This is the type of joke that earns its 8+ unambiguously.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I owe all my success and personal growth to this internship. It completely ruined my life.

jokes.text: After the Star Wars revelation, Ron asks: 'Is Star Wars the one with the little wizard boy?'
jokes.setup: Ron just delivered an intricate explanation involving Star Wars as a plot device.
jokes.punchline: He has absolutely no idea what Star Wars is — he only knew the date because he monitors cultural events that affect his associates.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The structure is flawless: Ron spent the previous 30 seconds being the most competent person in the room, meticulously tracking appendices and amendment dates and sleep patterns — and the entire reveal rests on a pop culture reference he doesn't even recognize. 'The little wizard boy' conflates Star Wars with Harry Potter in the most Ron Swanson way imaginable — he would only know enough to know there's a famous franchise with a young protagonist. The economy (eight words) and impact are maximum. This is the kind of joke that gets rewatched dozens of times.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I'm going to use my therapy technique. Three positive things: One, I have a job. Two, I have friends. Three, I'm not dead.

jokes.text: Station manager's credentials: 'I have six Lower Great Lakes Emmy Awards. I once sat in the original Batmobile. James Woods follows my niece on Twitter.'
jokes.setup: Hank Muntak warns Andy he'll regret walking out.
jokes.punchline: His list of credentials escalates from regional achievement to tenuous celebrity proximity — the last one being hilariously irrelevant.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is perfect: a semi-legitimate award → a cool anecdote → 'James Woods follows my niece on Twitter.' The third item is the comedic engine: (a) it's a Twitter follow, not even of him, (b) it's his niece, not him, (c) James Woods as the chosen celebrity is an inspired specific choice. The whole joke is about the pathetic indignity of measuring status by proximity to fame. Highly quotable, especially the third item.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You can't keep introducing yourself as Judge Perd Hapley.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: But I was a judge for one day.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You were a traffic court judge for four hours.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: Judge Perd Hapley.

jokes.text: Ben's Ice Town guilt spiral: 'It's Ice Town all over again.' (Beat.) Ron: 'Ben's right. This is Ice Town all over again.' Then: 'Ron!'
jokes.setup: Ben feels responsible for Leslie's mistake about the contract amendment.
jokes.punchline: Ron, usually a source of stoic reassurance, immediately validates Ben's worst self-accusation — prompting Leslie's exasperated 'Ron!'
jokes.explanation: Works as a callback to the show's long-running Ice Town gag AND as a character joke — Ron's blunt honesty is funny precisely when the situation calls for comfort. His confirmation of Ben's spiral followed by Leslie's single-word rebuke is perfectly structured.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: I have to be honest with you, I have no idea what's going on here. I don't understand the case, I don't understand the evidence, and frankly, I'm not even sure what this judge hammer does.

jokes.text: Ron's only contract: his Mulligan's Steakhouse club card, signed under the fake name 'Les Vegetables.'
jokes.setup: Ron advises always reading legal documents before signing — then reveals his own signing history.
jokes.punchline: His only contract is a steakhouse loyalty card, signed with a fake name that is a pun on 'les légumes' (vegetables in French) — the thing Ron hates most.
jokes.explanation: Possibly the most Ron Swanson joke imaginable: his only legal commitment is to a steakhouse. And the name 'Les Vegetables' — a fake name that is (a) a pun, (b) the word for the food he most despises, (c) somehow French — is inspired. This is a perfect character joke: every detail serves character AND is funny. The absurdity of choosing that specific fake name when infinite options existed speaks to his perverse humor. Strongly earns 9+ territory — it's a legendary character moment in miniature.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: As a journalist, I must say that this is a clear violation of... uh... the legal thing. The statute. The... *makes gavel sound* ...and that's the law.

jokes.text: April: 'I convinced her to quit.' Ben: 'Martha Stewart's apron line, my tomato plants— oh, God, I'm out! Where is my emergency list?'
jokes.setup: Ben learns April has driven away an intern and is about to yell at her
jokes.punchline: Ben desperately deploys his therapist's calming list technique in real-time stress, before he can even remember the items properly
jokes.explanation: A great payoff to the earlier calming-list joke. Ben running out of items and needing an 'emergency list' shows the technique is barely holding. 'My tomato plants' is a beautifully mundane calming item. The callback adds resonance and gets more laugh because we know the system from before.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I got the job! I'm gonna be making minimum wage!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's like, what, a thousand dollars a year? I'm rich!

jokes.text: April is told she would be 'a checkout girl at a gas station if it wasn't for that internship.' April: 'Yeah, I know.'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to give April a pep talk about the value of the Parks internship.
jokes.punchline: April's total absence of defensiveness — she completely agrees that she would have been a gas station clerk.
jokes.explanation: April's self-aware acceptance of this assessment — without any wounded pride — is a good character moment. Her lack of ego about her pre-Parks potential is both funny and surprisingly touching.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what your problem is, Andy? You don't believe in yourself enough.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Really? I think I believe in myself a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, you don't. You need to wake up every morning, look yourself in the mirror, and say 'I am going to have an amazing day.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow. That's... that's actually really good advice, Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Where do you come up with this stuff?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Fortune cookies.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley corrects Leslie: 'Well, Perd—' / 'It's Judge Perd.'
jokes.setup: Leslie begins to address him as she always has.
jokes.punchline: Perd insists on the honorific, with maximum self-seriousness, in his capacity as a TV judge.
jokes.explanation: Classic Perd pomposity. Short and functional. The joke is that 'Judge Perd' is a TV-show title he takes extremely seriously.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've systematized my therapy technique by alphabet. A is for avoidance, B is for bottling things up, C is for compartmentalization, D is for denial, E is for excessive sarcasm...

jokes.text: Perd Hapley: 'Now Leslie, I understand that what you've brought to the show isn't a box of objects but rather a symbolic box of allegations.'
jokes.setup: The TV debate begins
jokes.punchline: Perd has prepared an unnecessarily elaborate metaphorical reframing of the basic premise — as though 'symbolic box of allegations' is a profound legal concept
jokes.explanation: A mid-tier Perd Hapley tautology. The meta-description of the debate as a 'symbolic box of allegations' is well-chosen as a Perd-ism, but it's in the middling range of his character's jokes — functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.line: Oh my god, did you see what happened with those celebrities?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Which ones? Because I have VERY strong opinions about the situation with that one actor's third cousin's feuds with reality TV stars from 2009.

jokes.text: Perd attempts to summarize the situation: 'I think there are certain questions about certain aspects of certain parts of this situation that require an evaluation about whether or not this is or is not a valid argument.' Leslie: 'Extremely well-put.'
jokes.setup: Perd is supposed to provide judicial framing of the debate.
jokes.punchline: His statement contains zero information — it's pure sentence-shaped noise — and Leslie sincerely compliments it.
jokes.explanation: One of the great Perd moments. His statement is a masterpiece of saying absolutely nothing in grammatically correct English — 'certain questions about certain aspects of certain parts' is brilliant because the triple-'certain' reveals he has no specifics at all. Leslie's 'Extremely well-put' as a sincere response is the second layer of the joke. Both characterizations are perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I may have destroyed a delivery drone with my bare hands.

jokes.text: Perd: 'Okay, uh, I think there are certain questions about certain aspects of certain parts of this situation... that require an evaluation about whether or not... this is or is not a valid argument.' Leslie: 'Extremely well-put.'
jokes.setup: Perd is asked to weigh in on the legal debate
jokes.punchline: Perd says absolutely nothing in the most words possible; Leslie sincerely compliments it
jokes.explanation: A reliable Perd joke: maximum words, zero information. 'Certain questions about certain aspects of certain parts' is a perfectly calibrated content-free statement. Leslie's 'Extremely well-put' is the button that elevates it — her earnest sincerity is the second joke layered onto Perd's emptiness.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about Gryzzl, and I realize they have tentacles in every aspect of our lives. They know where we live, where we work, where we shop, what we like, what we don't like. They know everything about us.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: So I've decided to take them on. I'm going to fight Gryzzl with everything I have.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: First, I'm going to need some supplies. Do you have any orders for me?

jokes.text: Roscoe: 'Whoa! That's a serious allegaysh, homie.' Ben has just made a serious civic argument.
jokes.setup: Ben delivers a thoughtful argument about internet access being a necessity.
jokes.punchline: 'Allegaysh' — Roscoe's portmanteau of 'allegation' — applied to a measured civic argument, completely deflating the gravity.
jokes.explanation: Roscoe's slang truncations ('allegaysh', 'GryzzlPad out of here') are a consistent comic voice that satirizes tech-bro speech affectation. 'Allegaysh' is a specific and funny word. Good character voice.

jokes.text: Perd concludes: 'To be honest, Judge Perd is stumped by this case... I've also misplaced my judge hammer... Therefore, I must declare a mistrial, which is a term I've heard people use in the movies. Tap, tap, tap. Case ended.'
jokes.setup: Perd is supposed to render a verdict after a substantive debate.
jokes.punchline: He declares a mistrial because he's (a) stumped, (b) lost his gavel, and (c) only knows the term from movies. He then bangs the desk with the noise 'tap, tap, tap.'
jokes.explanation: Multiple distinct jokes stacked perfectly: (1) admitting he's stumped, (2) losing the gavel which he calls a 'judge hammer,' (3) citing movies as his legal precedent source, and (4) physically saying 'Tap, tap, tap' instead of actually banging a gavel. The 'judge hammer' is particularly inspired — it reveals he doesn't know what a gavel is. 'Case ended' as his formal ruling is a Perd Hapley classic. This whole sequence is character comedy at its finest.

jokes.text: Perd: 'Therefore, I must declare a mistrial, which is a term I've heard people use in the movies. Tap, tap, tap. Case ended.'
jokes.setup: Perd has to render a judgment
jokes.punchline: He declares a mistrial based purely on having heard it in movies, then mimes gaveling with three 'tap taps' instead of using an actual gavel
jokes.explanation: Perd's best moment in the episode. 'Which is a term I've heard people use in the movies' is an extraordinary acknowledgment of his own incompetence. 'Tap, tap, tap. Case ended.' as his substitute for a gavel is physically hilarious — he's using his finger or hand to tap a desk, completely committed to the format. The callback to the lost judge hammer makes 'tap tap tap' land even harder.

jokes.text: Andy announces he found a job as a janitor at the TV station paying minimum wage: 'Get this — they're gonna pay me the minimum wage.' Said with complete satisfaction.
jokes.setup: Andy walked out on his TV show negotiation and needs a new job.
jokes.punchline: He's proud to announce minimum wage as if it's a triumph.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Andy Dwyer characterization — his complete lack of financial ambition and genuine pride in minimum wage employment is a reliable character note delivered cleanly.

jokes.text: Tom explains how he got Andy the rights to Johnny Karate: by crying to the station manager about Lucy, Conrad, and Lucy's free dinners.
jokes.setup: Tom claims agent credit for renegotiating successfully.
jokes.punchline: His actual method was an emotional breakdown about his romantic jealousy — he essentially guilted the manager with vulnerability, and it worked.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff for the Lucy subplot — Tom's incompetent agenting accidentally succeeds because his emotional vulnerability was more persuasive than any business argument. The manager's 'Okay, fine, JUST STOP' is a relatable capitulation to an uncomfortable person.

jokes.text: April has replaced Jen with a whole group of new interns, found by doing what Leslie does — handing out flyers, canvassing, baking cookies. 'It was weird, I actually enjoyed finding them.'
jokes.setup: April sent away the one intern she liked (Jen) and needs replacements.
jokes.punchline: April accidentally enjoyed the wholesome activities she normally mocks — and reports this with mild horror.
jokes.explanation: A warm character moment that's also funny — April's reluctant admission that she enjoyed Leslie-style activities implies growth she can't quite admit to. 'It was weird' is the right tone.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional: 'That's actually really good advice for anything. If there's something that you want badly, you just have to believe that it's gonna work out.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just gotten his rights back through Tom's desperate negotiation
jokes.punchline: Andy frames the outcome as a result of positive belief rather than Tom's emotional manipulation of a station manager
jokes.explanation: Andy as an accidental philosopher delivering completely misattributed life wisdom is a reliable character beat. The gap between what actually happened (Tom's desperation + free meals) and Andy's takeaway (belief!) is the joke.

jokes.text: April adds: 'And I enjoyed bullying Jen into quitting.'
jokes.setup: April has just had a warm moment about enjoying the intern search.
jokes.punchline: She immediately undermines any growth with a reminder that she also enjoyed the dark half.
jokes.explanation: Perfect April button — any warmth must be balanced with menace. The contrast between the Leslie-like activities she enjoyed and the 'bullying' she also enjoyed is perfectly timed. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Ben suggests April should add 'telling people what to do' to her perfect job description. April's response: 'Good idea. You should up your therapy to seven times a week, stop dressing that way, and give me your wallet.'
jokes.setup: Ben gives April genuine career advice.
jokes.punchline: April immediately demonstrates 'telling people what to do' by issuing commands to Ben, including demanding his wallet.
jokes.explanation: The structure is perfect — April illustrates the advice by immediately acting on it, but her commands escalate from semi-reasonable ('more therapy') to petty ('stop dressing that way') to absurd ('give me your wallet'). The wallet demand as the capper is completely unexpected and very funny. This shows April's instinctive authority while being genuinely witty about it.

jokes.text: Ben's third therapy coping list: 'Victor Garber, James Garner, Jennifer Garner.' Then: 'I go alphabetical now.'
jokes.setup: April just robbed Ben. He deploys coping mechanism again.
jokes.punchline: All three items are 'Garner/Garber' — Ben has gone so deep into alphabetical systematization that he's now listing three adjacent names. Then the callback to 'I go alphabetical now' functions as a callback to a callback.
jokes.explanation: This is the best version of the running coping mechanism gag. Ben has gone so deep into his alphabetical system that he's listing three people with nearly identical names — Victor Garber, James Garner, Jennifer Garner. The repetition within the list (all Gar-) makes this a joke within a joke: he is BOTH calming himself AND OCD-organizing his calming list. 'I go alphabetical now' as the button is now a third callback and still lands. Earns its 8+ as the culmination of a well-developed running gag.

jokes.text: Tom reports to Lucy that while she was gone, he 'closed a bunch of deals, did a bunch of crunches.' He says this casually, as if these are equivalent.
jokes.setup: Lucy has returned. Tom tries to seem like he handled himself well.
jokes.punchline: The crunches make it in as a 'deal' — he's still performing for the Conrad competition in his mind.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the crunches made it into his professional summary. Confirms that the Conrad jealousy absorbed more of Tom's mental real estate than he'd admit. Economically placed.

jokes.text: Lucy breaks up with Conrad (off-screen). Then: she wants to talk about 'that shade Nicki Minaj threw at Jesse Eisenberg at the BAFTA awards.' Tom: 'He deserved it.' Lucy: 'No, he didn't!' Tom: 'Uh, settle in, because I have some very strong feelings about this.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Lucy finally seem to have a moment — the Conrad obstacle is removed.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a romantic beat, they immediately pivot to a heated celebrity gossip debate — their chemistry expressed through passionate pop culture arguments.
jokes.explanation: A warm and funny scene that subverts the expected romantic payoff. Their compatibility is shown through equal passion for celebrity gossip rather than a tender moment. 'I have some very strong feelings about this' as the final line is a perfect Tom line. The Nicki/Jesse Eisenberg BAFTA detail is a very specific fake celebrity incident that feels authentic.

jokes.text: Ron arrives at Leslie's house, having shot a Gryzzl drone out of the sky after it delivered a package addressed to his four-year-old son.
jokes.setup: Ron said earlier he has 'no reaction' to Gryzzl's activities and wouldn't help.
jokes.punchline: The moment they touched his child, he shot the robot and came to enlist. He's holding what is presumably a destroyed drone.
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff for Ron's arc in this episode. His earlier libertarian indifference ('I have no reaction to this') is completely abandoned the moment his child is touched — which is EXACTLY what you'd predict for Ron once you know his character. The act of shooting down a robot with presumably a firearm he had on hand is pure Ron. 'I destroyed the robot. No one is safe from these bastards. Tell me what to do, Leslie.' is a beautifully structured speech. The callback to his extreme child privacy concern (blacked-out photo) makes the payoff even richer.

jokes.text: Ron arrives with a destroyed drone: 'This is a flying robot I just shot out of the sky after it delivered a package to my house.'
jokes.setup: The episode has been building to Ron joining the anti-Gryzzl fight
jokes.punchline: Ron's entry into the alliance is that he physically shot a drone out of the sky — this is the proof of his grievance
jokes.explanation: Ron showing up with a destroyed drone he shot out of the sky is a perfect character payoff. Of course Ron Swanson would shoot a corporate drone. The escalation from 'I have no reaction to this' earlier in the episode to literally shooting down a robot that targeted his child is a superb character arc compressed into one episode. The physical evidence — he's brought the wreckage — makes it funnier. Justifies near-top scores.

jokes.text: Ron: 'No one is safe from these bastards. Tell me what to do, Leslie. I wanna help you take them down.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been ideologically opposed to helping Leslie fight a private company all episode
jokes.punchline: The moment his child is touched, all ideology evaporates and he becomes Leslie's soldier — a 180-degree character reversal earned through the entire episode
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode closer. The comedic payoff requires the full episode's setup: Ron's libertarian 'no reaction,' his paranoid redacted photo of his son, his dismissal of people who use 'doodads' — all of it funnels into the most earned possible reversal. 'No one is safe from these bastards' followed by a direct request for Leslie's orders is both funny and satisfying. The comedy comes from the absolute certainty that Ron Swanson would change nothing except for this specific thing. Near-perfect structure for an episode-length joke.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben suspect that Gryzzl is invading the privacy of Pawnee residents. April addresses the new Parks and Rec interns, while Tom helps Andy renegotiate a contract.
insight: Gryzzlbox's escalation comedy hits 82.6 with 60 jokes in 60 minutes—consistent density masks zero standout moments.
